  %\usepackage[utf8]{inputenc}

When you write a greta model, like so:


``` r
x <- as_data(seq(0, 1, length.out = 30))
y <- as_data(rnorm(30))

int <- normal(0, 10)
coef <- normal(0, 10)
sd <- cauchy(0, 3, truncation = c(0, Inf))

distribution(y) <- normal(int + coef * x, sd)

m <- model(int, coef, sd)
```

Your data stays bound to the model. You can't do:


``` r
data_values(m, y) <- rnorm(30)
#> Error in `data_values<-`:
#> ! `y` is not mutable data, so it cannot be replaced
#> ℹ Declare it with `as_data_mutable()` rather than `as_data()`
```


Usually, we don't need to do that, but sometimes it is useful to fit a model to many datasets.

This came up in greta issue #181 from user [@howardnewyork](https://github.com/howardnewyork):

> Is it possible to write a model, compile it, and then feed the compiled model
> different data sets? This is useful if you are running the same model over
> 100s of datasets.
>
> --- [greta issue #181](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/181)

This was always possible, but slow, as greta has to construct
the TensorFlow graph and TensorFlow has to trace it. Depending on what you were doing, this could really add up! We crafted a solution with: `as_data_mutable()`

## Declaring data mutable

Data normally enters greta under the hood as a TensorFlow *constant*. TensorFlow can fold a
constant into the graph, which makes it fast, but it also means the value is
baked in: changing it means building the graph again.

`as_data_mutable()` holds the data in a TensorFlow *variable* instead. The
graph reads a variable __by reference__, so replacing its value changes what the
model computes without rebuilding anything.


``` r
n <- 30
x <- as_data(seq(0, 1, length.out = n))
y <- as_data_mutable(rnorm(n))
```

Only `y` is declared mutable, because only `y` will be replaced. `x` stays
constant, and so do the numbers in the priors below.

We made this opt-in, as there is some cost to using variables like this, and
using constants is much faster. Essentially, variables have to be read, and copied out to
one batch per chain, on every evaluation, which can add up for larger data. Declaring
only what you will replace keeps that cost to the one array that needs it.

The rest of the model is written exactly as usual - you can run MCMC on this.
But we will talk about how to change out the data next.


``` r
int <- normal(0, 10)
coef <- normal(0, 10)
sd <- cauchy(0, 3, truncation = c(0, Inf))

distribution(y) <- normal(int + coef * x, sd)

m <- model(int, coef, sd)
```

## Fitting the same model to different data

To fit the same model to different data, use `data_values()`, specifically `data_values<-`.
This replaces the values behind a mutable greta array. The model
object is modified in place, so the next call to `mcmc()` uses the new data.

See for example:


``` r
simulations <- lapply(1:3, function(i) rnorm(n, mean = 2 * i))

estimates <- vapply(
  simulations,
  function(d) {
    data_values(m, y) <- d
    draws <- mcmc(m, n_samples = 300, warmup = 300, chains = 2, verbose = FALSE)
    mean(as.matrix(draws)[, "int"])
  },
  numeric(1)
)

round(estimates, 2)
#> [1] 1.75 3.30 5.69
```

The posterior mean of the intercept tracks the mean of each dataset, and the
model was built once.

Note that the loop takes its estimate from each fit *before* moving on. That is
deliberate. Because `m` is modified in place, it ends the loop holding the last
dataset, and a saved `draws` object still points at it. The draws are plain
numbers and keep their values, but `extra_samples()` resumes sampling against
whatever the model holds now — no errors, and carrying on against the wrong posterior, usually freezing because the step size was tuned for the old one.

If you need to keep whole fits rather than summaries, build a model per dataset.

## The dimensions must be the same as the original data

A TensorFlow variable has a fixed shape. That is the price of not retracing,
and greta checks it rather than letting TensorFlow raise a less helpful error
later:


``` r
data_values(m, y) <- rnorm(n + 1)
#> Error in `data_values<-`:
#> ! `value` must have the same dimensions as the data it replaces
#> ✖ We see dimensions: "31x1"
#> ℹ But we expect dimensions: "30x1"
#> ℹ Changing the dimensions would mean rebuilding the graph
```

> If you want to fit the same model to datasets with different dimensions
> (e.g. different numbers of observations) the easiest thing would be to write
> a function to build (and possibly fit) a greta model to a given dataset, then
> loop over that function feeding the datasets.
>
> --- Nick Golding, [on issue #181](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/181#issuecomment-394196667)

## data_values() must be used with as_data_mutable()

Data declared with plain `as_data()` is held as a constant, so it cannot be
replaced. greta says so, and names the fix:


``` r
data_values(m, x) <- seq(0, 2, length.out = n)
#> Error in `data_values<-`:
#> ! `x` is not mutable data, so it cannot be replaced
#> ℹ Declare it with `as_data_mutable()` rather than `as_data()`
```

## Other applications

The same mechanism is what **minibatching** needs. Minibatching means fitting to
a small random subset of the data on each iteration of an optimiser, rather than
all of it at once, so that a model can be fitted to data far too large to hold
in one graph. Each iteration needs a different subset swapped in, which is
exactly what `as_data_mutable()` does.

Nick Golding
[prototyped this on the greta forum](https://forum.greta-stats.org/t/sparse-matrix-format-for-count-and-binary-data-setting-dtype-of-tensors/124/8),
reaching into greta's internals to swap the data tensors directly. This is the
piece that was missing - the minibatching interface itself is still to come.

It is also what makes greta's own correctness checks affordable. Those follow
Geweke (2004): draw a fresh dataset from the model at every iteration and check
that the sampler recovers the prior. Rebuilding the graph for each new dataset
is the dominant cost of running them.

## References

Geweke, J. (2004). Getting it right: joint distribution tests of posterior
simulators. *Journal of the American Statistical Association*, 99(467),
799--804.
